text: Weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning.
explanation:
Everyone this side of heaven goes through night seasons: times of grief, confusion or depression when nothing makes sense, not even God. Sometimes we bring them on ourselves; often there's an enemy at work. Accusations always seem louder at night, just as a child's fever usually feels worst after dark.

But a night is only a night. Weeping is a temporary guest; joy is coming with the morning, and Joy is a Person. One day there will be "no night there" at all. Until then, He knows exactly what you're going through, and morning is on its way.

text: Right after his greatest victory, God told Abram, "Do not be afraid. I am your shield." Fear often comes after the win.
explanation:
Abram had just defeated four armies, received bread and wine from Melchizedek, been blessed by God Most High and given his tithe. The very next chapter opens: "After these things the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying, 'Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.'"

Why would he be afraid? Probably lying awake wondering whether those kings would come back for revenge. The enemy often attacks right after a high point. When you can't sleep, picture what God showed him: a shield all around you. Insecure people can't rest, but you are surrounded.

text: "He gives His beloved sleep," or as another translation reads, He gives to His beloved even while they sleep. Both are true.
explanation:
"It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows," that is, of worry and anxiety. Solomon wrote this, and God had named him Jedidiah, "beloved of the Lord." The Hebrew of the last line can be read two ways, and the rabbis debated it: God gives His beloved sleep, and He gives to His beloved in their sleep.

When you can't sleep, first settle that you're His beloved. Then, as you lie down, say, "Lord, what will You give me while I sleep?" Health renewed, wisdom imparted, problems worked on. Eve was formed while Adam slept. God does some of His best work while you rest.

text: "Judas went out immediately. And it was night." Whenever you turn your back on Jesus, it's night.
explanation:
John's Gospel has several night scenes. The first is Nicodemus, coming to Jesus by night to find the light. Then, in the upper room, Judas took the piece of bread from Jesus' hand and walked out to betray Him, "and it was night." Nicodemus came out of the night toward Jesus; Judas walked away from Jesus into the night.

Jesus said, "He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life." No matter how dark your circumstances, if you're turned toward Him, you're in the light. Darkness isn't where you are; it's away from Him.

text: Daniel spent the night in a den of hungry lions, and "no injury whatever was found on him, because he believed in his God."
explanation:
These weren't playful cubs. When Daniel's accusers were later thrown in, the lions overpowered them before they reached the floor. Daniel was there because he did right, praying to his God as he always had. Sometimes doing right lands you in a lions' den.

In the morning, the king found him untouched, and Scripture gives the reason: "because he believed in his God." Not because he fought, argued or strategised. When you're going through a night you don't understand, there's often nothing to do but believe. That's enough.

text: Jacob saw angels ascending and descending at night. Jesus said, "You shall see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man."
explanation:
Fleeing from his brother, Jacob slept with a stone for a pillow and dreamed of a ladder reaching heaven, with angels going up and down. It was night, and heaven was busy. In the New Testament, "at night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors" for the apostles.

Jesus told Nathanael He Himself is that ladder: heaven opened, angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man. Because you have Jesus, heaven is open over you and angels are active on your behalf, especially in your darkest hours.

text: Assyria's king lined his palace walls with his conquest of Lachish. There's no Jerusalem, because one night God struck down 185,000 of his soldiers.
explanation:
King Sennacherib had overrun Judah's fortified cities and sent a letter mocking Hezekiah's God. Hezekiah spread the letter before the Lord and prayed. "And it came to pass on a certain night that the angel of the Lord went out and killed in the camp of the Assyrians one hundred and eighty-five thousand." In the morning they were all dead.

The reliefs from Sennacherib's palace, now in the British Museum, proudly show the fall of Lachish. Jerusalem is nowhere to be seen. You may go to sleep with the threats roaring. God can turn it all around before you wake.
